title: Ines and the Well
premise: Mara Ashgrove, a pest controller whose real trade is keeping the town of Hollow Fen's old agreements intact, is called to the abandoned Well house where something leaves wet fingerprints on the inside of sealed doors. Every photograph in her grandmother's albums now shows an extra chair at the kitchen table, and Mara realizes the thing in the well has been claiming a seat in her family for generations. As the harvest moon approaches, she learns the founders' unfinished ritual requires a willing heir to name the well-thing and give it a place—or let it take one by force. In the end, Mara chooses to finish the ritual not alone but with Elise, the woman she loves and was ordered to keep away from the fen, binding the entity into memory rather than flesh, though the extra chair remains, empty and waiting.
about_author: Lior Reyes grew up in a coastal farming town where every family kept one story they never told twice. They write horror about inheritance, small towns, and the things we agree not to see.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Mara Ashgrove takes a routine pest complaint at the derelict Well house and finds fingerprints on the inside of a door nailed shut from without. Her POV establishes her rules: count the doors, keep the lights on, never stay past dark. The emotional beat is professional unease curdling into recognition—she knows these prints.

chapters.title: Counting Doors
chapters.summary: Back home, Mara inventories her grandmother's house out of habit and finds eleven doors where there should be ten. POV shifts briefly to her grandmother Ida, who counts them too and says nothing. The beat is dread disguised as domesticity; something has already entered the family's architecture.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Sorting photographs for Ida's failing memory, Mara discovers that every image from the last sixty years now includes an unfamiliar wooden chair at the kitchen table. Old prints, new chair. Her POV; the beat is vertigo—the past itself has been edited, and only she seems able to see it.

chapters.title: Hollow Fen's Ledger
chapters.summary: Mara consults the town archive and finds the founders' ledger: a ritual begun in 1897 to bind 'the tenant below' and left deliberately incomplete, renewed each harvest by an unnamed heir. Third-person limited on Mara. The beat is the horror of bureaucracy—a contract signed by ancestors she never agreed to.

chapters.title: Elise
chapters.summary: Elise Vann, archivist and Mara's secret partner, notices Mara's sleeplessness and pushes too close. Mara, bound by duty to keep loved ones away from fen business, lies badly. Elise's POV reveals she's been researching the Well house independently—and found her own family name in the ledger. Beat: love as liability.

chapters.title: Wet Footprints, Dry Floor
chapters.summary: The Well house calls again: footprints lead out of the dry well shaft across the floor and stop mid-room. Mara follows them to a child's drawing pinned to a beam—her own face, aged. Her POV. The beat is being known by something that has watched her whole life.

chapters.title: What Ida Remembers
chapters.summary: Ida surfaces from dementia into startling clarity and tells Mara about her sister Ruthie, who 'went to sit at the table' in 1963 and was never spoken of again. Ida's POV, fragmented and lyrical. The beat is grief resurfacing—the extra chair has held someone before.

chapters.title: The Founders' Rite
chapters.summary: In the archive cellar, Mara and Elise reconstruct the ritual: naming the tenant, offering it a defined place, sealing it with blood from the founding families' lines. Half the page is burned away. Shared POV alternating. The beat is reluctant partnership—duty forcing them together even as it forbids intimacy.

chapters.title: Nine Doors
chapters.summary: Ida's house loses a door overnight; the tenth is simply wall now, though everyone remembers it. Mara realizes the entity is renegotiating boundaries, room by room. Her POV. The beat is claustrophobia—the house itself is being edited, and Ida is sleeping nearer the kitchen each night.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Calendar
chapters.summary: Elise calculates the full moon falls in nine days, the same span as the founders' original rite. She confronts Mara about the lies and the ledger. Elise's POV. The beat is rupture and honesty—love declared openly against duty, raising the stakes for both.

chapters.title: Ruthie's Chair
chapters.summary: Mara finds Ruthie's belongings hidden in the crawlspace: a diary describing the rite's failure in 1963 because the heir refused to name the tenant, leaving it hungry and unnamed. Mara's POV. The beat is inherited guilt—her family chose silence, and silence fed it.

chapters.title: Fingerprints on the Window
chapters.summary: The entity reaches Ida's house directly: handprints bloom on the glass each dusk, closer to the kitchen window nightly. Ida, lucid again, tells Mara to run. Ida's POV. The beat is protective sacrifice—an elder trying to spend herself before the moon rises.

chapters.title: The Town That Forgot
chapters.summary: Mara canvases neighbors and finds no one remembers the Well house ever existed; the ledger pages are blanking as she reads. Only those with founder blood retain the memory. Her POV. The beat is isolation—the entity is erasing witnesses, and time is running out faster than she thought.

chapters.title: Blood and Water
chapters.summary: Testing the theory, Mara cuts her palm over the well shaft; the water rises to meet it, and a voice uses Ruthie's timbre to say her childhood nickname. Her POV, terror and tenderness tangled. The beat is seduction—the thing knows how to sound like love.

chapters.title: The Unfinished Page
chapters.summary: Elise deciphers the burned section using ultraviolet light: the rite requires the heir to offer the tenant a named place at their own table—not banishment but adoption. She hides this from the town council, who want a sacrifice instead. Elise's POV. The beat is moral choice—mercy versus expedience.

chapters.title: Council of Ashes
chapters.summary: The remnant council, led by the cold Mr. Halloway, votes to give the entity Ida as the 1963 rite intended. Mara refuses and is stripped of her office. Her POV. The beat is defiance—choosing family over institution, love over duty, at personal cost.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Mara and Elise prepare the kitchen: the extra chair centered, salt lines, Ruthie's diary open, Ida's blessing. Quiet chapter of domestic ritual and confession. Alternating POV. The beat is stillness before storm—two women setting a table for something terrible, together.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: The moon clears the fen and the well-thing comes up through the floors as rising water and reaching hands, wearing the faces of everyone it has taken. It sits in the chair. Mara begins the naming. Her POV. The beat is confrontation—terror held at bay by ceremony.

chapters.title: The Naming
chapters.summary: The entity offers Mara Ruthie's voice, then Ida's, demanding to be given a body. Instead Mara names it Tenant, gives it the chair, the photograph, the memory—a place in story, not flesh. Elise completes the seal with both their bloods. Shared POV. Climax: identity offered instead of a life taken.

chapters.title: What the Water Keeps
chapters.summary: The entity accepts the bound place and recedes, taking the wet cold with it—but the chair remains in every photograph, now simply part of the family record. Ida sleeps peacefully for the first time in chapters. Ida's POV. The beat is exhausted relief and ambiguous peace.

chapters.title: After the Moon
chapters.summary: Hollow Fen remembers nothing; the council forgets its vote; Mara rebuilds her life with Elise openly, no longer hiding. But she keeps counting doors, and there are ten again—one more than the plans say. Her POV. The beat is bittersweet normalcy, vigilance as devotion.

chapters.title: The Empty Seat
chapters.summary: Epilogue at Thanksgiving: Mara, Elise, and aging Ida set the table, and Mara places a plate at the extra chair out of respect rather than fear. In the final photograph, the chair holds a folded paper: thank you. Her POV closing the frame. The beat is haunted grace—some debts become inheritances, and love outlasts duty.
